doc.title: Bobby Gordon interviewed by Monk Rowe, Chautauqua, New York, September 12, 1997

title: The audience for traditional jazz and the craft of old songs
summary: Gordon says the audience is a small core, but lyrics and chord changes of 1920s and 30s songs appeal to younger listeners.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: It seems like there’s a small but enthusiastic core of jazz fans.

Yes. Especially the type that come here to Chautauqua. And you’ll see them in the audience tonight. And when there’s an intermission they’ll be out buying all the CDs because they’re the type of people that are the only ones left anymore for this type of music. Maybe there’s some young people coming up that like it, but it’s going to take a long time to train them.
To train them? See now there’s a key word I think. How do you train a future audience?

Well, I think that today’s music from the 30s and the 20s is coming back stronger and stronger. I’m not saying the big bands. I don’t think the big bands will ever come back. But I think the small group like Fats Waller’s and his rhythm, and I’m surprised that some black guys don’t form these type of bands like Fats Waller had in the 30s. Maybe they don’t think it’s right or something like that. But I know from experiences where I play, if we play something like “The Image of You” or an old Wingy Manone tune, and someone does a vocal on it, we get a very good response from the audience, which is a mostly younger audience. They’ve never heard these type of songs before. They’re listening to the lyrics again, and the lyrics are I think what knocks them out. I think that’s what they like. Because it makes them think well gee, what have I been missing you know? And I think that is the direction of jazz now.
Yeah. That’s an interesting thought. The lyrics and actual chord progressions in those days, well I supposed we can sound dated, but there seemed to be more of a craft to the songwriting.

Yes. They are not just one chord, like they have one or two chords and like they have today. These tunes were, you know, Gershwin and Irving Berlin and these guys, they wrote some pretty songs with nice chord changes and I think it’s the little melodies to them that please the younger generation’s ear. I think that’s what it is.
